title: A paired fit gave a lower inland seasonal sea-level contrast trend in Chesapeake than Delaware in 1991-2025
abstract: We tested whether seasonal mean sea level changed at the same rate inland and near the mouths of two estuaries. We used four NOAA gauges and 31 matched years from 1991 to 2025. We fit linear trends to September-minus-February mean level, then compared inland-minus-mouth trends. Chesapeake minus Delaware was -19.59 mm per decade, with conditional 95% three-year block-wild limits of -30.77 to -8.22. Each estuary trend alone was less certain: Delaware was +3.00 (-14.60 to 19.89), and Chesapeake was -16.60 (-33.77 to 0.30). Planned checks for block length, seasonal window, inferred values, nodal terms and record start retained negative difference intervals. The evidence shows a spatial difference under the fitted model. It does not identify a physical cause, a steady rate, a flood change or a forecast. Gauge selection, gaps, changing coastal gradients, source errors and short dependent records limit inference. The package contains original code, aggregate evidence, all uncertainty draws, a figure, source hashes, a retrieval script and arithmetic checks. Raw source responses remain external.

display.caption: Inland-minus-mouth September-to-February mean sea-level contrasts on 31 matched years, and fitted trends with conditional 95% three-year block-wild limits. The difference between estuaries is more precise than each individual trend. No causal inference is made.
